lessons.introduction: Start with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript basics. Draw your first object, then explain time-based rotation and local/world positions. Coordinates, axes, and angles are introduced here; WebGL and matrix calculations are not prerequisites. Each starter is an independent HTML document. Predict, edit one value, run, and record the observed numbers and reasons in the site notes. Reading a step or explanation does not replace your code; loading an example is a separate action.

steps.title: Draw a scene on a canvas
steps.explanation:
The starter is an HTML document with canvas and output elements. Inline style sets the canvas display size; JavaScript inside script type="module" draws the image. import * as THREE from 'three' exposes the library names under THREE. The site supplies the module, so no npm installation or external server is required.

document.querySelector('canvas') finds the canvas element in the document. output is selected in the same way; assigning a string to output.textContent displays it as text.

The canvas is the HTML element that receives the image. Scene groups 3D objects and Camera sets the viewing position and direction. WebGLRenderer uses them when renderer.render(scene, camera) draws to the canvas. Scene and Camera are not HTML elements. new creates an object; renderer.render(...) calls a method on an existing object.

Find canvas, scene, camera, and renderer in order. Check that the renderer receives the canvas selected from HTML. The camera is at (0, 0, 5), looking at the origin. There are no objects yet, so a background-only image is expected. In scene.background = new THREE.Color('#edf2f7'), change only the color to '#172554' and run. Record your prediction first.

draw reads canvas.clientWidth and clientHeight in CSS px. A zero width or height returns early to defer drawing. When you reopen the preview, ResizeObserver reports the size change and calls draw. observe(canvas) starts observation. At a positive size, setSize(w, h, false) fits the image, while camera.aspect = w / h and updateProjectionMatrix() apply the camera ratio. false leaves the CSS size intact. This supporting code appears in every step; keep it unchanged here. The next unit explores sizing, buffers, and DPR.

The + operators join strings and numbers in output. The canvas and output selectors each find one element in this document. Client dimensions are integers including padding but excluding borders and scrollbars; this canvas has zero padding and border. Observation and animation continue while the document remains mounted; running again replaces the iframe.
steps.solutionExplanation: scene.background is independent of the body background CSS. A changed value may leave an existing image unchanged until render runs again. If even the background is missing, read output and the error display, then check script execution, the canvas connection, and render in order.
steps.expected: The empty scene background changes from #edf2f7 to #172554. output shows the actual display width and height. Having no cube yet is expected.
hints: Check that the selected HTML canvas and the canvas in WebGLRenderer({ canvas }) are the same element.
After changing scene.background, check for renderer.render(scene, camera).
Assign new THREE.Color('#172554') to scene.background and render again.
questions: What do canvas, Scene, Camera, and WebGLRenderer each do?
Are scene.background and the body background CSS the same value?

steps.title: Your first cube and camera
steps.explanation:
This independent starter includes a cube. geometry = new THREE.BoxGeometry(1, 1, 1) defines its shape; material = new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ color: '#2563eb' }) defines the surface; cube = new THREE.Mesh(geometry, material) combines them into a scene object. This material is visible without lights, so no light is added.

Change only color in the material constructor and run. Then keep the color and change cube.position.x from 0 to 1. position is relative to the parent, initially Scene. With this camera, +X appears rightward and +Y upward, but screen directions depend on camera orientation. Temporarily comment out scene.add(cube), run, and restore it. Creation and scene connection are separate operations.

Restore cube.position.x to 0 and change the last argument of camera.position.set(0, 0, 5) to 7, changing camera.position.z from 5 to 7. Predict the cube's appearance from the more distant camera. Now change camera.position.set(0, 0, 5) to camera.position.set(2, 0, 5), keeping camera.lookAt(0, 0, 0). position sets location; lookAt sets the direction toward a world-space target. A camera initially looks along local -Z. lookAt does not move it to the target.

The completed example shows the final comparison: an orange cube and camera=(2, 0, 5). Test the intermediate x=1, z=7, and removed add separately in the starter, restoring each before the next test.
steps.solutionExplanation: create a Mesh from geometry and material, connect it to Scene, and render with a Camera that can see it. When z changes from 5 to 7 the perspective image is smaller, but the geometry width remains 1. near=.1 and far=50 define the drawing depth range. Keep them here; unit 03 explores clipping. If you place the camera inside the cube, do not mistake the blank image for missing lighting.
steps.expected: color changes the surface color; cube.position.x changes location. Removing add hides the cube. It appears smaller at camera.z=7. After lookAt, camera.position remains (2, 0, 5).
hints: Find Mesh creation and scene.add(cube) separately. Creation alone does not connect it to Scene.
Restore the cube to the origin and check that camera.z is 5 or 7.
Check location, direction, and drawing with camera.position.set(2, 0, 5); camera.lookAt(0, 0, 0); renderer.render(scene, camera);
questions: Why is a created Mesh invisible if it is never added?
What do position and lookAt each change?
Does moving the camera farther away change geometry width?

steps.title: Turn time into rotation
steps.explanation:
The starter contains the cube and camera and begins with speed=0, so it is stationary. Register the function with renderer.setAnimationLoop(renderFrame). The renderer later calls renderFrame(timeMs) each frame, passing the timestamp as its argument. A function passed for later invocation is called a callback.

timeMs is a timestamp in milliseconds. Save its first value in start and calculate elapsed seconds with seconds = (timeMs - start) / 1000. In cube.rotation.y = seconds * speed, speed is in rad/s. rotation uses radians: Math.PI is 180°, Math.PI / 2 is 90°, and 2 * Math.PI is one turn. Remember that camera.fov uses degrees instead.

Set speed to .5, run again, and read angle when output seconds is near 2. Run again with speed=1 and compare near the same 2 seconds. A frame might not occur at exactly 2 seconds; record the actual time and angle together. Adding a fixed angle per frame can make rotation per second depend on display refresh rate. This example calculates the angle from time.

renderFrame calls draw(). renderer.render(scene, camera) inside draw paints the updated rotation. Repeated calls reuse the same objects.
steps.solutionExplanation: .5rad/s for 2 seconds gives 1rad; 1rad/s for 2 seconds gives 2rad. Without converting 2000ms into seconds, the angle is 1000 times larger. renderer.render(scene, camera) must also run inside renderFrame after changing rotation. The same cube is updated, rather than recreated each frame. renderer.setAnimationLoop(null) stops repeated calls.
steps.expected: speed=0 is stationary. Near 2 seconds, speed=.5 gives angle≈1rad and speed=1 gives angle≈2rad. Both output and image change.
hints: Check whether seconds and angle both change. If only the numbers change, inspect render placement.
Check the division of timeMs by 1000 and the rad/s unit of speed.
Inside renderFrame, call renderer.render(scene, camera) after cube.rotation.y = seconds * speed.
questions: How does adding a fixed angle per frame differ from seconds*speed?
Why divide timeMs by 1000?
What should you check if numbers change but the image is still?

steps.title: Compare parent and child positions
steps.explanation:
This independent starter is stationary, with no animation. parent = new THREE.Group() is a parent node without its own shape. parent.position=(0, 0, 0), child.position=(2, 0, 0), and parent.add(child), scene.add(parent) connect them. The camera looks at the origin from (5, 4, 7) so that XZ motion is visible.

The tree is Scene → parent Group → child Mesh. child.position is local to parent; world position includes parent transforms in the coordinate system of the whole scene. angleInput has a string value, so convert it with Number(angleInput.value) before assigning parent.rotation.y. The choices are radian values 0 and Math.PI / 2.

world = new THREE.Vector3() stores the result. child.getWorldPosition(world) writes into world without modifying child.position. Predict both positions at rotation 0, then run: both are (2, 0, 0). Change parent Y rotation to Math.PI / 2 and compare again. Expect local=(2, 0, 0), world=(0, 0, -2). Point your right thumb along +Y; your curled fingers indicate positive rotation. In the XZ diagram, +X turns toward -Z.

The HTML range input has two values: 0 and 1.5707963267948966, the latter equal to Math.PI / 2. addEventListener('input', draw) calls draw when the value changes. toFixed(2) formats a number as a string with two decimal places. coordinates groups x/y/z for display without changing the position.
steps.solutionExplanation:
parent rotation turns the axes used to express the child's position. The child remains 2 units along the parent's +X. getWorldPosition applies the current parent transforms without requiring manual matrix multiplication. Values such as 1e-16 are floating-point results close to 0. Format output to 2 decimal places without rounding the actual position.

An object has only one parent. scene.add(child) after parent.add(child) removes child from parent. Record your predictions, actual coordinates, and reasons for both rotation conditions in the site notes.
steps.expected: parent stays at the origin. At parent.rotation.y=0, world=(2, 0, 0); at Math.PI / 2, world≈(0, 0, -2). child local=(2, 0, 0) is unchanged.
hints: Read child.position and world together in output and identify the value relative to the parent.
Check that the final connection is parent.add(child). scene.add(child) changes the parent.
Read with const world = new THREE.Vector3(); child.getWorldPosition(world);. Changing only parent.rotation.y to Math.PI / 2 gives local=(2, 0, 0), world=(0, 0, -2).
questions: Why is child.position unchanged when only the parent rotates?
Does getWorldPosition(world) modify child.position?
What changes if scene.add(child) is called last?

lessons.introduction: Match CSS display size, drawing buffer size, and camera aspect as separate concerns. Each independent HTML starter contains a front-facing BoxGeometry(1, 1, .2) and does not require previous code. stage has no padding/border; canvas uses display:block; width:100%; height:100%. The 240×240 and 480×240 conditions are examples when space permits. On narrow screens max-width can limit them; use actual w,h from output. Record shape proportions, CSS size, buffer size, and DPR in the site notes. Predict before running, change one item at a time, and use the site notes: conditions / prediction / actual image and numbers / reason for differences. The site supplies the three import; no separate installation is needed.

steps.title: Display size and buffer size
steps.explanation:
Initially DPR=1 and camera.aspect=1 in a square stage. renderer.setSize runs only once at startup. The camera looks from (0, 0, 5) toward the origin; the box has no rotation, making its front-face proportions easy to observe.

Use the size button to increase only stage width, then read CSS and buffer dimensions. stage.clientWidth/clientHeight use CSS px; canvas.width/height use buffer px. CSS can display the old buffer image over a wider area without drawing additional pixels. A changed display ratio can stretch the square horizontally.

In every example startWhenVisible uses requestAnimationFrame to wait for the first positive size, calls resizeScene once, then stops. A callback is a function the browser invokes before a later repaint; return ends this function call. This bootstrap does not observe later changes. addEventListener runs a function on click; assigning a CSS length string to stage.style.width changes display width only. reportSize reads current client and buffer dimensions and displays them through output.textContent. querySelector finds HTML elements; renderer.domElement is the same canvas supplied from HTML. In output, toFixed(4) formats a number as a string with four decimal places; + joins strings. Buffer pixel count is canvas.width × canvas.height.
steps.solutionExplanation: with a 240×240 buffer displayed at 480×240, the same image is stretched 2 times horizontally. If actual width differs from 480, substitute the output values. Read the actual stage size rather than body or window width. Automatic resizing is intentionally absent in this step.
steps.expected: stage width changes while canvas.width/height keep their initial values. The square can appear stretched. On narrow screens target and measured dimensions can differ.
hints: Read the CSS px and buffer px output rows separately.
Compare whether canvas.width changes after changing stage width.
Displaying a 240×240 buffer at 480×240 stretches it 2 times horizontally. Calculate the same ratio from your actual output.
questions: Does changing CSS width always change buffer width?
Why can stage width differ from window width?

steps.title: Match the buffer and camera separately
steps.explanation:
The starter resizeScene() reads w=stage.clientWidth, h=stage.clientHeight and calls renderer.setSize(w, h, false). The size button calls it, but camera.aspect is still 1. Choose a wide size and check that buffer dimensions match display dimensions. The square can still appear stretched.

After setSize in resizeScene(), add camera.aspect = w / h; camera.updateProjectionMatrix();. Compare the same sizes again. aspect is width/height; updateProjectionMatrix applies that ratio to projection calculations. Changing only one is insufficient.
steps.solutionExplanation: matching the buffer determines how many pixels are drawn. Camera projection determines the proportions used to place objects into that pixel region. With fixed vertical FOV, a wider view shows more of the scene horizontally without flattening objects. false in setSize prevents CSS display-size changes, not buffer changes.
steps.expected: setSize alone matches the buffer but can leave shape proportions wrong. Updating aspect and projection together preserves the front-face proportions.
hints: Compare display w/h with camera.aspect.
Check for updateProjectionMatrix after assigning camera.aspect.
Use renderer.setSize(w, h, false); camera.aspect = w / h; camera.updateProjectionMatrix(); before rendering.
questions: Why can a shape stretch even when the buffer size matches?
What does false prevent in the third setSize argument?

steps.title: Observe element size changes
steps.explanation:
This independent starter includes the completed resizeScene(). Now the size button only changes CSS and no longer calls resizeScene directly. The initial frame matches, but later stage changes do not.

Create observer = new ResizeObserver(resizeScene) and connect observer.observe(stage). ResizeObserver is a browser Web API, not Three.js. It calls the callback when an observed element changes size. Keep the initial resizeScene() call to size the first frame immediately.

Leave window dimensions unchanged and press the stage size button. The observer responds to the element's own size changes. Observe stage, which defines the size, rather than canvas. stage has no padding/border and canvas fills it at 100%, making the measurement basis clear.
steps.solutionExplanation: the observer does not understand cameras or buffers automatically. The resizeScene callback performs setSize, aspect and projection updates, and rendering. If dimensions oscillate, check false in setSize, canvas CSS, and that stage is observed. Use observer.disconnect() when observation ends.
steps.expected: Changing only the stage button matches measured dimensions, buffer, and aspect without resizing the browser window. resizeScene redraws the image too.
hints: Check output to see whether changing only stage CSS runs resizeScene.
Check that observer.observe receives stage rather than canvas.
Connect const observer = new ResizeObserver(resizeScene); observer.observe(stage); resizeScene();.
questions: Why can a window resize listener be insufficient?
Does the observer itself call render?

steps.title: Compare DPR 1 and 2
steps.explanation:
The starter includes resizing and starts with dpr=1. output displays actual CSS w,h, canvas.width/height, camera.aspect, and dpr. Change dpr to 2 and call renderer.setPixelRatio(dpr) followed by renderer.setSize(w, h, false). w,h must be CSS dimensions, not values already multiplied by DPR.

For a 240×240 CSS display, DPR 1 gives a 240×240 buffer and DPR 2 gives 480×480. Pixel count rises from 57,600 to 230,400, a factor of 4. For other display dimensions, use actual w,h. camera.aspect remains w/h without DPR multiplication.

The input value is a string, so Number(input.value) converts it to a number. The change event runs when the selection changes. Add renderer.setPixelRatio(dpr); at the DPR comment in resizeScene, then compare input values 1 and 2.
steps.solutionExplanation: DPR affects buffer resolution along both axes. It does not request making CSS display size or scene-object size 2 times larger. Although devicePixelRatio can vary by device or browser zoom, this experiment explicitly uses 1 and 2. A sharpness difference may be subtle and processing time is not necessarily 4 times greater. Multiplying DPR 2 times gives a factor of 4 along each buffer axis; inspect setSize arguments if that happens.
steps.expected: CSS size and camera.aspect stay unchanged. At DPR 2 each buffer axis becomes 2 times larger and pixel count becomes 4 times larger. A 240×240 display gives a 480×480 buffer.
hints: Record CSS px and buffer px side by side and calculate each axis ratio.
Check whether setSize receives w*dpr, h*dpr by mistake.
In renderer.setPixelRatio(2); renderer.setSize(w, h, false);, w,h are measured CSS dimensions. camera.aspect is w/h.
questions: Why does DPR 2 give 4 times as many pixels?
Should DPR also multiply camera.aspect?
Does 4 times as many pixels guarantee 4 times the processing time?

steps.title: Hide and show the stage
steps.explanation:
The starter has buttons to hide and show stage. After reading w,h near the start of resizeScene(), check if (w === 0 || h === 0) return;. output reports hidden dimensions without claiming a newly valid aspect.

Hide and show stage. With display:none, client dimensions can be 0. Do not divide w/h when h=0 or substitute 1 and label the result normal. The observer keeps watching stage and calls resizeScene when it has size again.

stage.hidden is a boolean property controlling visibility. Buttons and output are outside stage, so they remain usable while it is hidden. The hidden output aspect is the last valid value, not a newly computed ratio.
steps.solutionExplanation: return skips this size update. It does not disconnect the observer or terminate the program. After showing, setSize and aspect use the actual dimensions and render restores the image. To finish, record shape proportions and numbers for square/wide, DPR 1/2, and recovery from hiding.
steps.expected: Hidden dimensions are reported as 0 without division by 0. Showing stage restores finite aspect and current buffer dimensions while preserving shape proportions.
hints: Read whether stage.clientWidth/clientHeight become 0 while hidden.
Check that the zero-size guard precedes w/h.
Place setSize, aspect, projection, and render after if (w === 0 || h === 0) return;. The observer calls the same function after showing.
questions: How does replacing 0 with 1 differ from skipping an update?
Why can the image recover after the function returned?

lessons.introduction:
Compare the same scene with perspective and orthographic cameras. Change distance, FOV, near/far, and viewing target one at a time and explain why objects become smaller or disappear. Each independent HTML starter includes the resizing already introduced. No external GUI is required; labeled inputs and buttons support the baseline experiments. Restore the baseline before comparisons and record camera type, position, target, and projection values.

Record conditions / prediction / actual image and numbers / reason in the site notes. Selecting a step or opening explanations keeps your code. Only confirmed loading replaces it.

steps.title: Two objects at different depths
steps.explanation:
The starter contains A and B, both using BoxGeometry(1, 1, 1). A=(-1, 0, 2), B=(1, 0, -2); distinct colors and text names identify them. camera=(0, 0, 9), lookAt=(0, 0, 0), fov=50, near=.1, far=30. Neither cube is rotated.

Read object and camera coordinates in output and predict which appears larger. A's center is at camera depth 7; B's is at depth 11. A world z value is not itself camera depth. This camera looks along -Z from z=9, so 9-2=7 and 9-(-2)=11.

Do not resize B to match A. Observe the unmodified objects. Perspective projection makes closer objects appear larger. Both geometry widths remain 1; only projected widths differ. Keep the x positions so the objects do not obscure each other.

querySelector finds DOM elements and textContent displays strings. coords uses toFixed(2) for display strings without changing positions. Blue A is on the left, orange B on the right; use A/B names and coordinates as well as color. scene → A, B is the object tree. This step is observation; keep both geometries unchanged.

Sizing is supplied support code. resizeScene reads stage.clientWidth/clientHeight in CSS px and returns at zero. A continuous ResizeObserver redraws after hidden preview becomes visible or changes size. setPixelRatio(1) fixes experimental DPR; setSize(w,h,false) preserves CSS. Update perspective aspect and orthographic bounds separately, then updateProjectionMatrix and render. The 240×240 / 480×240 buttons change stage.style.width; max-width may reduce actual width in a narrow preview. Record actual CSS/buffer output. input.value is a string, read with Number. change/click listeners connect committed inputs and buttons; press Apply after editing numbers. HTML min/max/step and checkValidity check the input ranges.

querySelectorAll collects numeric inputs. [...collection] makes an array; the every callback checks each input.checkValidity(). Any invalid input displays an error and returns. event.target identifies the changed select or checkbox; value/checked read its selection. hidden controls zoom visibility; disabled prevents editing the unused FOV input in orthographic view. String converts the initial distance to the string used by input.value.
steps.solutionExplanation: this difference is caused by projected depth, not geometry size or material. If you rotate the camera, the simple 9-z calculation no longer generally applies. Restore the baseline before comparing.
steps.expected: Of the two objects of width 1, A at camera depth 7 appears larger than B at depth 11. output shows actual object and camera coordinates.
hints: Distinguish geometry width from projected width. Both geometries have width 1.
Use camera.z=9 and object z values to check the front-facing depths 7,11.
Restore A=(-1, 0, 2), B=(1, 0, -2), camera=(0, 0, 9) for the baseline where A appears larger.
questions: Why do equal geometries have different image sizes?
Does B at z=-2 have camera depth -2?

steps.title: Camera distance and FOV
steps.explanation:
This starter contains the same cubes and a restore-baseline button. applyCameraSettings() converts inputs with Number before applying them. The baseline is camera.z=9, fov=50. Keep the two experiments separate.

First hold fov=50 and change only camera.z from 9 to 13, retaining the origin as the lookAt target. Compare how both objects shrink. Their center depths become A=11, B=15. Restore the baseline, keep camera.z=9, and reduce only fov from 50 to 30. Call camera.updateProjectionMatrix() after assigning fov.

FOV is the vertical viewing angle in degrees. A smaller FOV shows a narrower area at larger image scale from the same position. Moving the camera closer may look similar, but relative sizes at different depths are not always identical.

After the input experiments, edit code too: change baselineDistance = 9 to 13 and run. Restore 9, then change baselineFov = 50 to 30. The solution starts at distance 9/FOV 30; inputs can restore the 9/50 reference.
steps.solutionExplanation: moving changes A/B center depths from 7/11 to 11/15. FOV changes projection scale while keeping position and depths fixed. Recording both only as zoom misses this difference. If FOV input has no effect, check the camera passed to render and its projection update.
steps.expected: At camera.z=13 both objects shrink and their relative size difference changes. After restoring, fov=30 enlarges both while position and depths remain 7/11.
hints: Check output for fov=50 in the distance experiment and camera.z=9 in the FOV experiment.
Check updateProjectionMatrix after assigning camera.fov.
Restore the baseline and use camera.fov = 30; camera.updateProjectionMatrix(); for FOV only. The distance experiment uses camera.position.z = 13.
questions: Do distance movement and FOV changes always match across multiple depths?
Does changing FOV also move camera.position?

steps.title: Orthographic projection and magnification
steps.explanation:
The starter has subjectCamera and ortho cameras, with only activeCamera passed to render. Both use position (0, 0, 9) and the origin as target. Perspective FOV and orthographic bounds are different settings, so the overall scene scale need not match exactly at the switch.

The orthographic settings are halfHeight=3, left=-halfHeight*aspect, right=halfHeight*aspect, top=halfHeight, bottom=-halfHeight, near=.1, far=30. Compare A/B sizes, then move ortho.position.z from 9 to 13. Keep orientation, bounds, and zoom=1 fixed, with objects inside the clipping range.

Restore distance 9, change ortho.zoom from 1 to 2, and call ortho.updateProjectionMatrix(). Orthographic magnification is set by bounds or zoom rather than distance. On resize, retain halfHeight, recompute left/right from the new aspect, and update projection. Assigning ortho.aspect is not a solution.

Projection selects activeCamera as subjectCamera or ortho. The zoom input appears only for orthographic view. The solution starts at orthographic distance 9/zoom 2. Reset restores perspective 9/50 and orthographic half-height 3/zoom 1 together. FOV is disabled in orthographic view; use zoom to magnify.
steps.solutionExplanation: under orthographic projection, equally sized objects with the same orientation do not shrink with depth. Moving the camera to change depth alone retains image size. zoom=2 narrows the visible range and enlarges objects. Orthographic images can still stretch if resizing is omitted.
steps.expected: A and B appear equally sized in orthographic mode and keep their sizes as camera.z changes 9→13. zoom=1→2 enlarges both. Changing stage proportions preserves shape proportions.
hints: Check that activeCamera is the selected ortho.
Compare the left/right versus top/bottom range ratio with stage w/h.
Keep halfHeight=3, set left/right=±halfHeight*aspect and top/bottom=±halfHeight, then call updateProjectionMatrix.
questions: How is orthographic magnification determined?
Why is assigning camera.aspect insufficient for an orthographic camera?

steps.title: Near and far clipping
steps.explanation:
The starter restores the perspective baseline: camera=(0, 0, 9), A=(-1, 0, 2), B=(1, 0, -2), near=.1, far=30. Controls are off. near/far are front/back planes at camera-space depths, not spheres at distances from the origin. Keep .1>0 and far>near.

Change near from .1 to 7 and then 8, calling updateProjectionMatrix each time. A's center depth is 7, but a cube is not a point. With side length 1 its surface depths span [6.5, 7.5]. near=7 clips part of A; near=8 puts all of A in front of the near plane so it disappears. B spans [10.5, 11.5] and remains.

Restore the baseline, hold near=.1, and change only far from 30 to 9. Predict which cube disappears and record the actual image with its settings. Do not use only the center to claim that near=7 hides A completely.

Apply near/far inputs after editing. For an invalid range, read the inline error and restore near>0 and far>near. The solution starts at near=8, far=30; reset before comparing partial clipping.
steps.solutionExplanation: far=9 includes A's depth range but lies before B's range, so B disappears. Clipping does not delete an object from Scene. Restoring near/far shows it again. A perspective near value extremely close to 0 can reduce depth precision; choose a range that is needed. Do not use near=0 for this perspective camera.
steps.expected: near=7 clips part of A; near=8 hides A. After restoring near=.1, far=9 hides B. Restoring the settings shows both objects again.
hints: Distinguish A center depth 7 from surface range [6.5, 7.5].
Check projection updates on the current activeCamera after near/far changes.
near=8, far=30 hides A but retains B. near=.1, far=9 retains A but hides B.
questions: Why does near=7 not hide all of A?
Is an extremely small near always better?
Has a clipped object been deleted from Scene?

steps.title: Camera target and OrbitControls
steps.explanation:
This independent HTML explicitly imports { OrbitControls } from 'three/addons/controls/OrbitControls.js'. controls = new OrbitControls(activeCamera, canvas) connects a camera and the canvas receiving events. controls.target is a world-space target, initially (0, 0, 0). Apply target.set(0, 0, 0) with controls.update().

From the baseline, use left drag and the wheel while comparing camera.position, controls.target, and object positions in output. Dragging orbits the camera rather than rotating the objects. The wheel primarily changes perspective camera distance or orthographic zoom. Inputs and buttons also support baseline distance/target/projection experiments, so required tasks do not rely only on mouse interaction.

Change enableDamping from false to true and call controls.update() in the loop. Inertia needs updates each frame. In numeric comparison mode, disable interaction with controls.enabled=false and also guard loop updates with if (controls.enabled) controls.update(). On camera switches, dispose old controls, create controls for the new activeCamera, and apply target and update.

Edit damping = false to true and run. The loop already includes if (controls.enabled) controls.update(). Numeric comparison sets enabled=false and stops loop updates. Apply disposes and reconnects controls to clear residual inertia, then applies numeric position/target. Camera X and target X allow keyboard comparison of position and viewing direction. Uncheck comparison to resume pointer interaction. setAnimationLoop receives the function called each frame. coords reads the three position numbers; output also reports object rotations.
steps.solutionExplanation: if lookAt and controls both set orientation each frame, the last call can overwrite the earlier one and make the view jump. Use target consistently while controls manage orientation. enabled=false does not cancel every explicit update call. If switching cameras still moves the old one, inspect which camera was passed to the controls constructor.
steps.expected: Dragging changes camera.position while object positions stay the same. Output shows distance changes for perspective wheel interaction and zoom changes for orthographic interaction. With damping=true, loop updates continue the motion.
hints: Read which changes in output: object position or camera.position.
Check update after target changes and every frame with damping.
On camera switches use controls.dispose(); controls = new OrbitControls(activeCamera, canvas); controls.target.set(0, 0, 0); controls.update();.
questions: Are controls.target and camera.position the same value?
Why can calling lookAt and controls.update every frame make the view jump?
What should you check if switching cameras still moves the old camera?

steps.title: Observe the frustum from outside
steps.explanation:
This starter has subjectCamera for the image and overviewCamera for outside observation. One canvas alternates between them without split viewports. subjectCamera=(0, 0, 9), near=.1, far=12, fov=50. overviewCamera observes from (10, 8, 16). far is reduced from 30 to 12 so the whole frustum can be observed; object depth ranges [6.5, 7.5], [10.5, 11.5] still fit.

Find scene.add(subjectCamera), helper = new THREE.CameraHelper(subjectCamera), and scene.add(helper). The helper is a direct scene child, not a subjectCamera child. Set helper.visible=false in subject view and true in overview. visible hides lines without deleting the object.

Select overview and reduce subjectCamera.fov from 50 to 30. Call subjectCamera.updateProjectionMatrix() followed by helper.update(). Restore the FOV and change only near or far to observe the front/back planes. Check names so the inputs update subjectCamera rather than overviewCamera.

Also edit baselineFov = 50 to 30, run, then select overview. The solution has FOV 30; compare line width with 50. View changes only activeCamera, keeping subjectCamera as the input target. subjectCamera is added before helper, so its world transform updates first during overview rendering. resizeScene updates aspect for both subject and overview cameras.
steps.solutionExplanation: a frustum is the camera's visible volume; for perspective it resembles a pyramid with its tip cut off. A smaller FOV narrows it; near/far move its front/back planes. Do not expect the full frustum to be visible through the same camera. CameraHelper references subjectCamera.matrixWorld, so connecting subjectCamera to scene also updates its transform while overview is rendered. Omitting helper.update after camera settings change can leave lines showing the old projection.
steps.expected: Overview displays the subject frustum. fov=30 is narrower than fov=50; near/far changes move front/back planes. Subject view lets you compare actual clipping.
hints: Distinguish the current overview view from the input target subjectCamera.
Check that both subjectCamera and helper are added directly to scene.
Call subjectCamera.updateProjectionMatrix(); helper.update(); then renderer.render(scene, overviewCamera) to observe from outside.
questions: Why is it difficult to see the whole frustum through subjectCamera itself?
What do helper.update and camera.updateProjectionMatrix each update?
Why add subjectCamera to scene when rendering from overview?

lessons.introduction:
Separate the parent origin and child offset to build spin, orbit, and a hinge. Check predictions at fixed angles before combining time-based motion. Each starter HTML includes Scene, camera, and resizing without requiring your previous draft. In unit 01 the parent was at the origin; here pivot=(1, 0, 0) adds parent translation. Angles use radians. The final Euler-order experiment is supplementary; quaternion implementation is not required.

The site supplies the three import. canvas is the drawing surface; output shows actual object values. Use querySelector to find a DOM node by id; input.value is a string, Number converts it to a number, and textContent writes text. An addEventListener callback runs after a button click. syncInputs initializes inputs from the scene state, so editing a source constant also updates the controls. Apply reads all shown controls; Reset restores the source baseline. Number.isFinite and checkValidity reject missing or nonfinite numbers. String converts a value for input; toFixed formats a number as text without changing coordinates. Tiny floating-point differences need tolerance, not exact equality. The for...of loop checks each input.

steps.title: Axes and object origins
steps.explanation:
The starting tree is Scene → pivot Group → body Mesh. pivot.position=(1, 0, 0), body.position=(2, 0, 0), and all rotations are 0. body uses BoxGeometry(1, .6, .4), so symmetry does not hide orientation changes. The camera looks toward the origin from (6, 4, 8).

scene.add(new THREE.AxesHelper(3)) shows scene axes; pivot.add(new THREE.AxesHelper(1)) shows pivot axes. +X is red, +Y green, and +Z blue. Read text axis names and values as well as colors. Moving the camera changes the directions these axes appear to point on screen.

Compare body.position with body.getWorldPosition(world). Predict local=(2, 0, 0), world=(3, 0, 0), then run. Position here means the Mesh origin, not that all surface points have the same coordinate.
steps.solutionExplanation: the parent origin is already translated 1 unit along world +X. The child is another 2 units along parent +X, giving world center 3. Each helper follows its parent transform, so their origins differ too. The difference from unit 01 world=(2, 0, 0) is caused by the changed parent location.
steps.expected: pivot origin is world=(1, 0, 0), body local=(2, 0, 0), and body world=(3, 0, 0). Scene and pivot axes have different origins.
hints: Check the tree to confirm that body belongs to pivot.
Check the stationary case where parent position 1 adds to body.position 2.
Use pivot.position.set(1, 0, 0); body.position.set(2, 0, 0); pivot.add(body); scene.add(pivot); and read getWorldPosition.
questions: Why is world 3 while local is 2?
How does adding AxesHelper to scene differ from adding it to pivot?

steps.title: Spin about the object origin
steps.explanation:
This starter includes the same tree and fixes pivot.rotation.y=0. Keep body.position=(2, 0, 0) and change only body.rotation.y from 0 to Math.PI / 2. Input is in radians; do not assign 90 directly.

Predict which changes: body orientation or the world position of its origin. Compare the cuboid's long direction with the axes and read getWorldPosition. Distinguish seeing an object turn from seeing its center move.

For a source edit, find const bodyAngle = 0 and set it to Math.PI / 2. The body.rotation.y assignment uses that constant; input and Reset use the same source baseline. You can also compare with the body local Y input and Apply.
steps.solutionExplanation: body.rotation changes orientation about the body's local origin. Its parent-relative position remains (2, 0, 0), so its world origin stays at (3, 0, 0). Geometry does not change. A cuboid rather than a cube makes the orientation difference after 90° easier to see.
steps.expected: body orientation changes, but local=(2, 0, 0) and world=(3, 0, 0) remain unchanged. pivot angle is 0.
hints: Read body and pivot angles separately in output.
Check that you change body.rotation.y rather than body.position.
Compare pivot.rotation.y = 0; body.rotation.y = Math.PI / 2;. The body world origin stays at (3, 0, 0).
questions: Why can orientation change while the origin stays fixed?
Why does assigning 90 not mean 90°?

steps.title: Orbit about the parent origin
steps.explanation:
This independent starter restores body.rotation=0. Keep pivot.position=(1, 0, 0) and body.position=(2, 0, 0), changing only pivot.rotation.y from 0 to Math.PI / 2. Predict local and world positions separately before changing it.

The offset 2 units along parent +X rotates with the parent. Positive 90° about +Y turns +X toward -Z. Starting from parent origin (1, 0, 0), move 2 units along -Z to reach body origin (1, 0, -2). Compare getWorldPosition with the XZ diagram.

For a source edit, change const pivotAngle = 0 to Math.PI / 2. The pivot.rotation.y assignment, initial input, and Reset share that source baseline. The pivot Y input is an alternative experiment.
steps.solutionExplanation: if child offset is 0 there is no orbit radius. Rotate the parent to turn the offset direction. Rotating only body produces the previous spin. Parent rotation also turns body orientation; do not describe this as a circular path with world orientation fixed.
steps.expected: At pivot.rotation.y=0, body world=(3, 0, 0); at Math.PI / 2, world≈(1, 0, -2). body local=(2, 0, 0) stays fixed.
hints: First check whether the rotated object is body or pivot.
Check that body.position.x is 2 rather than 0.
With body.rotation.y = 0; pivot.rotation.y = Math.PI / 2;, local=(2, 0, 0) and world=(1, 0, -2).
questions: Why does an offset of 0 remove the orbit path?
Does parent rotation change only body position?

steps.title: Combine spin and orbit
steps.explanation:
This starter includes the same hierarchy and time-based renderFrame, initially stationary with orbitSpeed=0 and spinSpeed=0. seconds is elapsed time since the first timestamp. Distinguish pivot.rotation.y = seconds * orbitSpeed from body.rotation.y = seconds * spinSpeed.

Enable only orbitSpeed=.5 and observe, then restore it to 0 and enable only spinSpeed=1. Finally enable both. Predict parent and child-local angles near 2 seconds and compare output. Both speeds use rad/s.

Apply starts time from zero with the current speeds; Reset restores the speeds written in the source. In renderFrame, the first timestamp is stored in startTime and elapsed milliseconds are divided by 1000. undefined means no timestamp has been stored yet.
steps.solutionExplanation: with orbitSpeed=.5 and spinSpeed=1, at about 2 seconds the parent angle is about 1rad and body local rotation is about 2rad. The body local angle does not describe the whole world orientation because parent rotation also applies. Do not generalize simple addition from this same-Y-axis example to arbitrary axis combinations. Update the existing objects rather than creating a new Mesh each frame.
steps.expected: Parent-only rotation orbits; body-only rotation spins. Both enabled produce simultaneous motion. Near 2 seconds pivot≈1rad and body local≈2rad; compare with the actual output time.
hints: Enable one speed at a time to identify each motion.
Check that seconds is in seconds rather than ms.
Use pivot.rotation.y = seconds * .5; body.rotation.y = seconds * 1; before renderer.render(scene, camera).
questions: Does body.rotation.y alone describe its whole world orientation?
Can simple addition about the same Y axis be generalized to every axis combination?

steps.title: Build a hinge at the door edge
steps.explanation:
This step is an independent door example. BoxGeometry(2, 3, .15) has width 2 centered at the origin. Initially hinge.position.x=0 and door.position.x=0, connected with hinge.add(door), scene.add(hinge). First compare center rotation at 0 and Math.PI / 2.

Restore angle 0 and apply both hinge.position.x=-1 and door.position.x=1. The parent moves to the left edge while the door center moves right by half-width 1 relative to the parent. Check that the closed world center remains (0, 0, 0), then change hinge.rotation.y to Math.PI / 2.

Read hinge-origin and door-center world coordinates in output and observe the fixed edge. Do not translate geometry or edit vertices. Unlike the body spin example, the parent origin is outside the object center to change the rotation pivot.

For a source edit, set const hingeX = -1 and const doorX = 1; then change const hingeAngle from 0 to Math.PI / 2. These constants feed the position/rotation assignments and the inputs. Alternatively edit hinge X, door local X, and hinge Y and press Apply. Reset restores the constants currently written in the source.
steps.solutionExplanation: the closed center is -1+1=0. At 90° the door center becomes (-1, 0, -1), while the hinge origin stays (-1, 0, 0). Moving only hinge to -1 with door offset 0 changes the closed position too. For width 4, the same rule gives hinge=-2, door=+2. To finish, record world values for spin/orbit and the fixed door edge in the site notes.
steps.expected: After setting the hinge, angle 0 gives door center world=(0, 0, 0). At Math.PI / 2, the center is≈(-1, 0, -1), while the hinge stays at (-1, 0, 0).
hints: Check that half of width 2 is 1 and the left edge is -1.
Check both offsets: hinge=-1 and door=+1.
Compare hinge.position.x = -1; door.position.x = 1; hinge.rotation.y = Math.PI / 2;. Leave geometry unchanged.
questions: Why change both parent and child offsets?
For door width 4, what should hinge and door x values be?
Are geometry vertices and Object3D transforms the same thing?

steps.title: Supplement: order of two-axis rotations
steps.explanation:
This supplementary starter stops animation and parent rotation and shows a cuboid and axes that make orientation clear. Fix body.rotation.x=Math.PI / 4, body.rotation.y=Math.PI / 3, body.rotation.z=0. The default order is 'XYZ'.

Keep the three angles and change only body.rotation.order from 'XYZ' to 'YXZ'. Compare orientations and explain why three numbers alone may not fully define a rotation. Euler order specifies intrinsic local-axis rotation order. Do not describe it as always rotating world X then world Y.

For a source edit, change const eulerOrder = 'XYZ' to 'YXZ'. You can also select Euler order and press Apply. The numeric angles remain fixed.
steps.solutionExplanation:
rotations about multiple axes can produce different results in different orders. This order-change experiment does not preserve the old world orientation. Quaternion conversion and gimbal-lock solutions are not required. For a question about translation after rotation, stay within the introduced contract: position.x is relative to parent axes. Do not mix it with the separate local movement method translateX if that method has not been introduced.

Next come geometry vertices, normals, and shared resources, followed by lighting/materials/textures, models/selection, and animation/performance/cleanup. Units 05~28 in the roadmap are planned for self-contained practice improvements, not already completed revisions.
steps.expected: With x=Math.PI / 4, y=Math.PI / 3, z=0 unchanged, XYZ and YXZ produce different orientations. This supplement does not add quaternion implementation to the first four units required completion.
hints: First check that parent rotation and animation are 0.
Keep all three angles and change only order.
Set body.rotation.order = 'YXZ' and render. Observe the intrinsic local-axis order difference.
questions: Why can order matter even with identical x/y/z values?
Does changing order preserve the old world orientation?

lessons.introduction: Build position arrays and distinguish vertices from triangles. Predict each change and record actual images and numbers in the site notes. Every example is independent HTML.

steps.title: Build a triangle from attributes
steps.explanation: The second Float32BufferAttribute argument, 3, is the number of components x,y,z per vertex. Nine components give position.count=3. Change topY from 0.2 to 1 and compare the top corner and triangle area. setAttribute attaches the attribute under position.
steps.solutionExplanation: The vertex count stays fixed while the top corner moves. With a null index, every three consecutive positions form one triangle. Float32BufferAttribute stores a floating-point array for the GPU.
steps.expected: 3 vertices, no index, 1 triangle; topY changes from 0.2 to 1.
hints: Find the topY constant.
Keep itemSize at 3.
questions: How would the count change with itemSize=2?

steps.title: Connect two faces with four vertices
steps.explanation: The starter uses six positions for a square, duplicating two corners. Use four vertices and setIndex([0,1,2,0,2,3]) as in the solution to build the same faces. Sketch the zero-based vertex numbers and compare them with the arrays. Enter 0,1,99 in the HTML index-array field and apply it: the error must preserve the previous shape. Every index must be below position.count. Reapply the original array to recover.
steps.solutionExplanation: index.count=6 does not mean six stored vertices. Three indices make one face, so there are two faces. Corners with different UVs or normals still need separate vertices.
steps.expected: Starter: 6 vertices, no index. Solution: 4 vertices, 6 indices. Both show a two-triangle square.
hints: The solution position array has 12 components.
Connect 0,1,2 and 0,2,3.
questions: What do index.count and position.count count?

steps.title: Validate a vertex update
steps.explanation: Accept vertex numbers 0–2 and y from -2 to 2. Apply vertex 4 and verify the previous triangle survives the error. Then apply vertex 2 with y=0.2. The starter changes the CPU array but leaves the rendered shape stale. Change notifyGpu=false to true.
steps.solutionExplanation: setY modifies the array. needsUpdate=true requests GPU upload and increments version. Recompute boundingSphere to avoid stale bounds. Reject invalid indices and empty input before mutation.
steps.expected: Vertex 4 is rejected without mutation. A valid edit updates CPU and image and increments version.
hints: Inspect needsUpdate after setY.
Set notifyGpu to true.
questions: What is missing when only the CPU value changes?

lessons.introduction: Compare triangle facing separately from the normals used for lighting. Keep camera and lighting fixed while changing one condition.

steps.title: Index order and front faces
steps.explanation: The camera looks from +Z toward the origin. The starter [0,2,1] is clockwise from this view, so its FrontSide face is invisible. Change it to [0,1,2]. Check that computeVertexNormals also changes normal.z from -1 to +1.
steps.solutionExplanation: Vertex order determines facing. Flipping only a normal does not restore a culled face. MeshBasicMaterial isolates facing from lighting in this experiment.
steps.expected: Starter is invisible with normal.z=-1; solution is visible with normal.z=1.
hints: Keep the positions fixed.
Swap the second and third indices.
questions: How do normals differ from facing?

steps.title: Light a surface with missing normals
steps.explanation: The starter uses four vertices and six indices for two folded faces. It has no normal attribute, but r186 automatically falls back to flat shading for MeshLambertMaterial, so the faces remain visible. Set calculateNormals=false to true and compare shading across the shared edge and normal.count.
steps.solutionExplanation: computeVertexNormals accumulates adjacent-face contributions at shared vertices and normalizes them. normal.count becomes 4; the first normal is approximately (-0.192,-0.192,0.962). Missing normals do not necessarily mean black surfaces. Compare the r186 flat fallback against interpolated vertex normals.
steps.expected: normal.count changes 0→4; the shared vertex normal is about (-0.192,-0.192,0.962), and shading across the fold changes.
hints: Find calculateNormals.
Enable the computeVertexNormals call.
questions: Why does brightness change without moving the light?

steps.title: Smooth shading across shared vertices
steps.explanation: Keep the sphere geometry and light fixed; change only flatShading from true to false. The starter has abrupt brightness changes across triangles; the solution interpolates normals smoothly. computeVertexNormals accumulates adjacent face contributions at indexed shared vertices.
steps.solutionExplanation: flatShading derives face normals in the shader. false interpolates vertex normals. Duplicated corners such as BoxGeometry edges remain split even after computeVertexNormals. Changing flatShading after compilation also requires material.needsUpdate=true.
steps.expected: Vertex/index counts and first normal stay fixed; only flatShading true→false changes shading across triangle boundaries.
hints: Keep sphere segmentation fixed.
Change only flatShading to false.
questions: How do duplicated vertices affect normal averaging?

lessons.introduction: Use === to inspect which resources two Mesh objects share. Predict object transforms separately from geometry and material edits.

steps.title: Two objects sharing resources
steps.explanation: a and b are distinct Mesh objects sharing geometry and material. Change stretch=1 to 1.5: a.geometry.scale stretches both boxes. Also compare changing only a.position.x, which leaves b in place.
steps.solutionExplanation: geometry.scale changes the shared vertex array. Mesh position and scale are per-Object3D transforms and do not mutate geometry. The output reports actual bounding-box heights and reference equality.
steps.expected: Geometry/material references are shared. Both heights change from 1 to 1.5 while centers stay at x=-1,1.
hints: Change only stretch.
Inspect a.geometry.scale(1,stretch,1).
questions: How does a.scale.y differ from a.geometry.scale?

steps.title: Inspect Mesh.clone resource sharing
steps.explanation: b=a.clone() creates another Mesh but retains geometry and material references. In the starter, b.geometry.scale and b.material.color.set also affect a. Set isolate=false to true to assign geometry.clone and material.clone first.
steps.solutionExplanation: Cloning resources makes only b orange and 1.6 high; a stays blue and 1 high. geometry.clone also copies attribute arrays. A material clone would still share textures, but this example uses no textures.
steps.expected: Starter: both references true, both orange/height 1.6. Solution: false, a blue/height 1, b orange/height 1.6.
hints: Clone both resources in the isolate branch.
Clone before editing.
questions: Why does Mesh.clone retain shared resources?

steps.title: Separate only the material
steps.explanation: Keep geometry shared and clone only b.material for independent color. Set separateMaterial=false to true. After changing b to orange, verify a stays blue and geometry=== remains true.
steps.solutionExplanation: Clone only the resource requiring independence. Sharing is a per-reference choice. Cleanup uses Sets to dispose each shared resource once. Run the example again after pressing Release resources.
steps.expected: Solution shares geometry but not material: a blue, b orange, both heights 1.
hints: Do not add geometry.clone.
Clone b.material before changing its color.
questions: Must geometry also be cloned to separate color?

lessons.introduction: Compare three light types using the same sphere and MeshLambertMaterial. MeshBasicMaterial does not react to these lights. Change one input at a time and record the bright region.

steps.title: Uniform ambient light
steps.explanation: The starter AmbientLight intensity is 0, leaving a black sphere. Change intensity to 1 and apply it through the HTML input too. Moving the light position cannot create directional shading for ambient light.
steps.solutionExplanation: Ambient light contributes equally in all directions. The blue material becomes visible, but curvature is less distinct than under directional lighting. AmbientLight cannot cast shadows. This input restricts intensity to nonnegative values.
steps.expected: Intensity 0→1 brightens the sphere without a directional highlight.
hints: Find the intensity constant.
Compare intensities 0 and 1 first.
questions: Does moving ambient light shift the bright side?

steps.title: Directional position and target
steps.explanation: The directional light at (2,2,3) points toward its target. Change targetX from 0 to 4 and observe the bright side move while the light position stays fixed. The HTML input also edits target.x. Add light.target to the scene so its world transform updates.
steps.solutionExplanation: The light travels along target.position-light.position. The output normalizes that vector. Light rotation does not define its direction. Both objects are direct Scene children here, so local and world positions match.
steps.expected: Light position stays (2,2,3); target.x changes 0→4, flipping the direction x sign and moving the bright side.
hints: Keep light.position fixed.
Change only light.target.position.x.
questions: Would changing only rotation have the same effect?

steps.title: Point-light distance and brightness
steps.explanation: Keep PointLight intensity=20 and decay=2. Change z from 4 to 2 and compare front-face brightness. The input accepts 1.5–8 so the light stays outside the sphere. Position changes both attenuation and incidence direction, unlike ambient light.
steps.solutionExplanation: distance=0 removes the range cutoff, not attenuation. With decay=2, light weakens with distance. Material, curvature, and output conversion affect pixels, so halving z does not make every displayed pixel exactly four times brighter.
steps.expected: Intensity and decay stay fixed; z=4→2 brightens the front face. distance stays 0.
hints: Find pointZ.
Keep intensity at 20.
questions: How do distance=0 and intensity=0 differ?

lessons.introduction: Keep the left sphere as a reference and change one variable on the right. Camera, lights, color, and geometry match. The environment is generated from a small coded room; no external HDR is required.

steps.title: Compare only roughness
steps.explanation: Both spheres begin at roughness=.8, metalness=0, envMapIntensity=1. Change the right roughness constant to .15. Compare the broad blurred reflection on the left with the sharper reflection on the right. The HTML input also changes only right roughness.
steps.solutionExplanation: roughness in 0–1 changes the spread of reflection, not base color or light intensity. PMREM prefilters environment lighting for different roughness values. The geometry segmentation remains fixed.
steps.expected: Left stays .8; right changes .8→.15. metalness=0 and environment intensity=1 stay fixed while reflection shape changes.
hints: Find the constant assigned to material.roughness.
Keep metalness at 0.
questions: Is roughness the same as sphere triangle count?

steps.title: Compare only metalness
steps.explanation: Fix roughness=.8 and environment intensity=1. Change right metalness from 0 to 1. Compare reflection color between the dielectric on the left and metal on the right. Both use #b98245; for the metal this color tints surface reflection.
steps.solutionExplanation: metalness=0 is dielectric and 1 is metal; intermediate values can represent mixed surfaces. Metal does not brighten through dielectric diffuse response. Judge the reflection and color under fixed lighting, rather than brightness alone.
steps.expected: Left metalness stays 0, right changes 0→1. Both roughness values stay .8 and environment intensity stays 1.
hints: Change only metalness.
Check equal roughness values in output.
questions: What can make a metal appear dark?

steps.title: Separate environment light from background
steps.explanation: Both spheres use roughness=.8 and metalness=0 and explicitly share the same PMREM texture in material.envMap. The right envMapIntensity starts at 0. Set environment to 1 to match the left. The visible #edf2f7 background is separate from environment lighting.
steps.solutionExplanation: scene.environment supplies a default environment for standard materials without an envMap; scene.environmentIntensity controls that default. Here both materials have an explicit envMap so only right material.envMapIntensity changes. PMREMGenerator.fromScene captures a separate scene. Dispose the generator after generation and the shared returned target once at final cleanup.
steps.expected: Right environment intensity 0→1 makes both spheres match. Background and directional light stay fixed.
hints: Set environment to 1.
Keep scene.background fixed.
questions: How do environment maps and visible backgrounds differ?

lessons.introduction: UV connects image locations to vertices; world coordinates place objects. Use an original 8×8 PNG and real TextureLoader to separate coordinate mapping, repetition, and recovery.

steps.title: Reduce only the UV range
steps.explanation: The plane has world width 3.6. Change uvScale=1 to .5. Also apply U range .5 through the input. The left half of the image should cover the entire plane without changing mesh position or scale.
steps.solutionExplanation: U and V identify horizontal and vertical image locations, usually in 0–1. Halving U stretches the left image half across the same world surface. Position and UV attributes are separate arrays.
steps.expected: Maximum U 1→.5; world width remains 3.6. Only blue and yellow cover the plane.
hints: Change uvScale to .5.
Read the uv attribute, not position.
questions: What do UV and world coordinates each control?

steps.title: Connect repeat counts to wrapping
steps.explanation: The repeat inputs already contain 4,2, but the starter uses ClampToEdgeWrapping. Enable RepeatWrapping and apply. Compare stretched edge colors with four horizontal and two vertical image copies.
steps.solutionExplanation: repeat multiplies UV coordinates. wrapS and wrapT determine how coordinates outside 0–1 are sampled. Clamp extends edge colors; RepeatWrapping repeats the image. Set needsUpdate after changing wrapping on an uploaded texture.
steps.expected: repeat=[4,2] stays fixed; both axes change clamp→repeat, producing 4×2 quadrant tiles.
hints: Enable the RepeatWrapping checkbox.
Check both wrapS and wrapT.
questions: Why can repeat 4,2 still stretch edge colors?

steps.title: Recover from an invalid image
steps.explanation: The starter loads corrupt data PNG and displays an error. Change loadImage(invalid) to loadImage(sample). Select real PNG and JPEG files, then try a corrupt image and restore the sample.
steps.solutionExplanation: TextureLoader decodes asynchronously. Only a successful result replaces material.map; failures keep the last valid image. Dispose replaced or failed textures and revoke object URLs on success, failure, or cleanup. Selected files belong only to this running iframe and cannot be restored from backup.
steps.expected: error→ready with an 8×8 sample. Inputs survive decode errors and sample recovery works. Re-run requires file reselection.
hints: Pass sample to the initial loadImage call.
A corrupt file with a PNG extension still fails decoding.
questions: Which resources do Texture.dispose and URL.revokeObjectURL release?

lessons.introduction: The same byte 128 has different meaning as color and as roughness. Separate decoding into the Linear-sRGB working space from final display encoding. Tone mapping is disabled and neutral lights stay fixed.

steps.title: Annotate a color image as sRGB
steps.explanation: The original 2×2 gray image encodes sRGB color 128. Change inputSpace="none" to "srgb". Also apply srgb through the selector and compare brightness.
steps.solutionExplanation: Annotating a color map with SRGBColorSpace decodes sRGB into the linear working space. NoColorSpace instead treats 128/255 as already linear, making display output brighter. MeshBasicMaterial avoids lighting so this experiment isolates color conversion.
steps.expected: NoColorSpace→srgb. The same source byte produces approximately 188→128 at output.
hints: Find inputSpace.
Keep the output at srgb.
questions: Why can input colorSpace change brightness without changing bytes?

steps.title: Preserve numeric roughness data
steps.explanation: The green channel 128/255 encodes a roughness coefficient, not color. Change inputSpace="srgb" to "none" and compare reflections under a fixed point light. Keep roughness=1 and metalness=.25.
steps.solutionExplanation: roughnessMap multiplies material.roughness by the green channel. NoColorSpace preserves that numeric value. Incorrect sRGB decoding changes .502 to about .216, narrowing reflections. normalMap also encodes numeric direction components and uses NoColorSpace. This experiment runs roughnessMap and explains the separate normalMap role.
steps.expected: NoColorSpace preserves 128/255≈.502, spreading the reflection. Color-image rules do not apply to every texture.
hints: Select none for numeric data.
Consider green multiplied by roughness=1.
questions: What direction information would sRGB decoding damage in a normal map?

steps.title: Separate working space and output encoding
steps.explanation: Use Linear-sRGB (.5,.5,.5) directly on a plane without an image. Change renderer.outputColorSpace from LinearSRGBColorSpace to SRGBColorSpace. Also apply srgb through the selector.
steps.solutionExplanation: Three.js performs lighting and color calculations in Linear-sRGB. outputColorSpace controls final encoding and does not repair texture semantics. Linear .5 displays as about 188 on a normal sRGB display. Distinguishing input, working, and output stages avoids double conversion.
steps.expected: Working .5 stays fixed; linear→srgb output changes approximately 128→188. NoToneMapping remains enabled.
hints: Find renderer.outputColorSpace.
material.color .5 is a linear value.
questions: Why does compensating for bad input through output settings break other colors?

lessons.introduction: Shadows require renderer, light, caster, and receiver settings together. Keep box, floor, and light fixed while testing shadow presence, camera clipping, and map resolution separately.

steps.title: Connect caster and receiver
steps.explanation: renderer.shadowMap.enabled, light.castShadow, and floor receiveShadow are already true. Change caster.castShadow=false to true. Enable the castShadow input, apply, then disable only receiveShadow for comparison.
steps.solutionExplanation: A caster writes depth from the light viewpoint. A receiver compares that map to determine blocked light. Either missing flag can remove the shadow. Receiving a shadow is separate from casting one.
steps.expected: cast false→true adds a floor shadow. receive false removes it again.
hints: Find caster.castShadow.
Check why the light and renderer also need flags.
questions: Which four settings should you check when a visible object has no shadow?

steps.title: Fix clipping with the camera frustum
steps.explanation: Keep mapSize=512 and change extent=.5 to 4. Apply half extent 4 through the input. Enable the helper to see the depth region expand to include the box and floor. After recovery, compare half extents 8 and 4 to inspect finer edges over narrower coverage at the same map resolution.
steps.solutionExplanation: Directional-light shadows use an orthographic camera. Only the region inside left/right/top/bottom and near/far enters the depth map. Update its projection matrix and helper after changes. Raising mapSize cannot recover missing coverage.
steps.expected: Half extent .5→4; mapSize stays 512. The clipped shadow recovers and the helper region expands.
hints: Change all four side planes.
Compare coverage while keeping resolution fixed.
questions: How do missing shadow regions differ from blocky shadow edges?

steps.title: Compare resolution at fixed coverage
steps.explanation: Keep extent=4 and change mapSize=32 to 512. Apply 512 through the input and compare blocky edges. Then explain how wider and smaller camera regions divide the same map pixels.
steps.solutionExplanation: 32→512 increases each side 16 times and texel count 256 times. Depth storage and render cost may rise. BasicShadowMap avoids filter blur. Dividing 8 world units by the map width changes units/texel from .25 to .015625.
steps.expected: Half extent stays 4; actual map changes 32×32→512×512. Distinguish resolution from repairing camera clipping.
hints: Set both map dimensions.
Dispose an existing map and set it to null so the next draw allocates the new size.
questions: How do mapSize and camera extent trade quality against cost?

lessons.introduction: Convert client coordinates into canvas NDC and cast a ray from the camera. Use overlapping boxes and their distance list to select the nearest object after margin and size changes.

steps.title: Compute NDC from the canvas rectangle
steps.explanation: The starter normalizes by innerWidth/innerHeight. Change canvasRelative=false to true. Click center and top-left, press Change margin and width, then click center again.
steps.solutionExplanation: getBoundingClientRect returns the current canvas client position and CSS size. NDC x is 2*(clientX-left)/width-1. Since up is +1, y is 1-2*(clientY-top)/height. Do not confuse CSS dimensions with buffer pixels or window size.
steps.expected: Center NDC≈(0,0); top-left≈(-1,1). Center still selects front after margin/width changes.
hints: Set canvasRelative to true.
Read a fresh rectangle on every click.
questions: Why can dividing by canvas.width fail with DPR or page margins?

steps.title: Select the first distance-sorted hit
steps.explanation: The input array is [back,front]. The starter chooses the last hit. Change nearest=false to true and click the overlapping center. Compare every reported name and distance.
steps.solutionExplanation: intersectObjects sorts intersections by distance from the ray origin, independently of input array order. hits[0] is nearest. A shared triangle edge can yield two coincident hits on one object, so hit count is not object count.
steps.expected: The list puts front before back; selection changes back→front.
hints: Use hits[0].object.
Do not repair this by reversing the input array.
questions: How does recursive=true differ from choosing the nearest object?

steps.title: Clear selection on empty space
steps.explanation: Change clearOnMiss=false to true. Select front, then click empty top-left space. Change margin and width, select front again, and also try Clear selection.
steps.solutionExplanation: Selection connects intersections to application state. An empty list sets null and restores original colors. Each box owns a distinct material here, preventing selection color from propagating. Ray computation and highlight updates serve separate purposes.
steps.expected: Center selects green front; an empty click selects none and restores orange.
hints: Call highlight(null) when there are no hits.
Connect independent materials to unit 07.
questions: Does Raycaster decide whether a missed click keeps the previous selection?

lessons.introduction: Connect shared materials, surface color, asset errors, and ray selection from units 07, 09, 10, and 13 to a GLB model. glTF describes scenes, meshes, materials, and clips; GLB packages JSON and binary data into one file. Each step is an independent HTML document with two original panels. Predict before changing one condition, then record actual values, images, and reasons in site notes.

steps.title: GLB loading state and recovery
steps.explanation:
Import GLTFLoader from the same 0.186.1 installation as core. loader.parseAsync(buffer, "") reads an ArrayBuffer and resolves a Promise with scene and animations. status remains loading until await completes, then becomes ready or error. Loading and error text are HTML elements, readable even without WebGL objects.

This starter intentionally reads corrupt bytes, so re-running repeats the failure. Select static and click Load sample. Alternatively change the final sample('invalid') to sample('static') in the editor and run. Load textured to see the embedded 2×2 PNG on both panels. Try corrupt GLB again and confirm that the old model and HTML controls survive.

File input uses file.arrayBuffer(). Only self-contained GLB up to 2 MiB is accepted; external URIs and Draco/Meshopt/KTX2 are rejected before parsing. Multi-file .gltf is unsupported. Selected files exist only during this run and are excluded from backups. Reselect after re-run, reload, or restore. Restoring code/notes does not restore the selected file.
steps.solutionExplanation: Remove the old model only after the replacement parses successfully. Failed requests preserve it. A request number rejects stale successful results and releases their real resources. This unit observes success/error recovery; unit 24 studies reversed completion order.
steps.expected: The starter reports error. Loading static gives ready and meshes=2. textured displays four colors; another corrupt input preserves the model and selection UI.
hints: Check that the model selector and buttons remain usable after an error.
Re-running repeats corrupt input too. Explicitly choose and load static.
Change the final sample('invalid') to sample('static') to change startup.
questions: What recovery problem results from removing the old model before parsing?
Why must a file be selected again after restoring a backup?

steps.title: Select model descendants
steps.explanation:
A GLB scene is a parent containing meshes. Passing only [root] with recursive=false misses its children because the parent has no triangles. Change recursive to true and click the left panel. NDC uses the current canvas rectangle; hits[0] is the nearest intersection.

Also select Left and Right from the object list. Both the list and ray call the same highlight function. Click empty space or Clear selection to restore color. Repeat with textured and after a file failure. The list displays names, while selection uses actual object references from the current meshes array.
steps.solutionExplanation: recursive=true tests descendants. Reading the canvas rectangle on every click preserves coordinates after resize. Replacing the file rebuilds the list for the current model and clears the old highlight.
steps.expected: With false, ray clicks miss while the list works. With true, clicking Left/Right turns only that object orange.
hints: Distinguish root from its descendant Mesh objects.
Change recursive separately from NDC.
Set const recursive=true and compare clicks, the list, and empty space.
questions: If the list works but ray selection fails, what would you inspect?
How should old object references be handled when replacing a model?

steps.title: Highlight and restore shared materials
steps.explanation:
Both static panels reference the same mesh and material indices in GLB. Check shared at load=true and material identity. With isolateMaterial=false, changing one shared color turns both panels orange.

Set isolateMaterial to true. Selection clones original material and assigns it only to the selected mesh. Before switching to Right, restore Left's original material and dispose the highlight clone. Clearing selection should restore blue and shared identity. In textured, original and clone still share map references, so clearing a highlight must not dispose the map.
steps.solutionExplanation: clone separates the material, not its textures. Restoring selection before replacement/cleanup allows original resources to be deduplicated in Sets and released once. Dispose resources releases actual geometry/material/texture and renderer and ignores repeated calls. Use the site Run action to create a new iframe for another experiment.
steps.expected: With false, one selection changes both colors. With true, only the selected panel changes; switching or clearing restores colors and shared identity.
hints: Check whether the two materials are === before selection.
Assign the clone only to the selected Mesh.
Set isolateMaterial=true and compare Left → Right → Clear selection.
questions: Which resources remain shared after material.clone()?
Why is disposing the texture with the old highlight clone a problem?

lessons.introduction: Continue perspective cameras from 03 and GLB loading from 14. Frame a distant model by looking at its world-bounds center, without moving the model to the origin. Box3 is an axis-aligned bound, not the surface itself. Read center, size, camera distance, and clipping separately, then record predictions and actual results.

steps.title: World center and size
steps.explanation:
offset is a GLB with both panels scaled by 8 and centered at (40,-15,3). After root.updateWorldMatrix(true,true), box.setFromObject(root) computes world bounds including descendants and parent transforms. getCenter(center) and getSize(size) write into supplied Vector3 objects without moving the model.

With useCenter=false the starter looks at the origin, leaving the model off-screen. Set useCenter=true. Read center≈(40,-15,3), size≈(30.4,12.8,0), and check that camera.x/y match the center. Alternate static and offset to verify 8× world size. An axis-aligned Box3 can contain empty space around rotated surfaces.
steps.solutionExplanation: Use the world center for controls.target and camera position instead of moving the model. Placing the camera along +Z from that center gives a front view of this static scene. Model coordinates remain unchanged.
steps.expected: false shows background; true centers the distant model. static size is about (3.8,1.6,0), offset about (30.4,12.8,0).
hints: Distinguish local position from world center.
getSize is max-min, not distance from the origin.
Set useCenter=true and compare center with camera.x/y.
questions: Why does lookAt(0,0,0) miss a far-offset model?
Does computing Box3 move the model?

steps.title: Fit camera from FOV and aspect
steps.explanation:
Use the same offset model. useFov=false fixes distance at 7 and clips the large model. Set useFov=true, enter margin=1.25, and click Fit camera. A bounding sphere uses r=size.length()/2. Convert vertical FOV to radians; horizontal FOV is 2*atan(tan(vFov/2)*aspect). Use the smaller FOV in d=r/sin(fov/2)*margin for a conservative sphere fit.

ResizeObserver updates aspect and projection at positive CSS sizes, then refits. On mobile, read whether distance grows as horizontal FOV narrows. near=max(d-2r,.00001) and far=d+4r leave depth room. Filling the view and preventing near/far clipping are different conditions.
steps.solutionExplanation: FOV is in degrees while Math.sin takes radians. Using vertical FOV alone can clip sides in a portrait view. Sphere fitting is conservative rather than optimal for each shape, but contains this bound from every direction.
steps.expected: At distance 7 only part is visible. With useFov=true and margin 1.25 the whole model fits; a narrower view increases camera distance.
hints: Do not fix d to the model size.
Check that the smaller of vFov and hFov is used.
Set useFov=true and margin 1.25, then compare both widths.
questions: Why does distance grow as aspect decreases?
How is near/far selection different from FOV fitting?

steps.title: Empty bounds and recovery
steps.explanation:
empty is valid GLB with no drawable Mesh. When box.isEmpty() is true, read the empty-model message separately from load failure. guardEmpty=false keeps fitting an empty bound and moves the camera to a tiny distance near the origin. Set guardEmpty=true to return early.

Load static after empty, then empty again. Check that the last valid camera is preserved. Test a tiny local GLB, or temporarily add root.scale.setScalar(.001) before root.updateWorldMatrix in fitModel. A minimum radius .001 prevents a zero-size point bound from producing zero distance/near. An empty model and a very small model are different states.
steps.solutionExplanation: isEmpty checks bounds with min greater than max. Zero size alone does not imply empty. File and sample controls remain live after empty/error states and can recover with a valid sample.
steps.expected: A successful ready parse can also have empty=true. With guardEmpty=true the camera is preserved across empty loads, and static restores visible geometry.
hints: Compare status for empty and corrupt GLB.
Check for an early return before fitting empty bounds.
Set guardEmpty=true and record camera coordinates for static → empty.
questions: Is a zero-size bound identical to an empty bound?
How does preserving the camera help recovery from an empty model?

lessons.introduction: Continue sizing, OrbitControls, and camera fitting from 02, 03, and 15. target is the orbit center; damping continues motion after input. Read frames to compare continuous and on-demand rendering. This model has no animation, so idle rendering can stop.
